blocks.note: surface reading: a nobleman of high standing
setter's reading: one particular eighteenth-century marquis, a celebrated general whose name hangs on many English pub signs

explanation.walkthrough: The Marquis of Granby was a British commander in the Seven Years' War; so many inns were named after him that he became a byword.
explanation.definitionFit: The title Marquis of Granby belongs to the heirs of the Dukes of Rutland, the famous holder being the general John Manners.

clue.text: Incline calves as to golden calf

definitions.text: Incline calves as to golden calf

blocks.note: surface reading: bending the lower legs, as in a kneeling act of worship
setter's reading: the Israelites bowed before the golden idol in Exodus, bending the knee in reverence

explanation.surface: Worshippers bend their legs before the golden calf idol of Exodus.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is on calf twice: the back of the leg, which bends when you kneel, and the idol the Israelites worshipped.
explanation.definitionFit: To genuflect is to bend one knee briefly in worship, so bending the legs before an idol describes it.

clue.text: Table is transformed by a flower

indicators.note: something transformed has changed its form, so the letters of the preceding word plus its neighbour take a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the anagram signal in the surface

explanation.surface: A dinner table is transformed by setting a flower on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is does double duty: its letters join the fodder while it also reads as part of the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Astilbe is a garden perennial with feathery plumes of tiny blossoms, a specific example of the general class named.

blocks.note: Lavengro is the semi-autobiographical novel by George Borrow, so its author supplies the name
a dale is a valley, a dip in the land

explanation.surface: The hero of a Victorian travel novel takes a swim in the Lake District.
explanation.walkthrough: Lavengro (1851) is George Borrow's wandering memoir; the Lakes means England's Lake District, where Borrowdale is a well-known valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowdale is a valley, a hollow among the Cumbrian fells, lying south of Derwentwater in northern England.

blocks.note: surface reading: an ordinary question about the novelist's activities
setter's reading: that year Zola published his open letter J'accuse over the Dreyfus affair

explanation.surface: A history quiz question about the French novelist Émile Zola's doings in one particular year.
explanation.walkthrough: J'accuse means I accuse, the headline of Zola's 1898 letter charging the French army with framing Dreyfus.
explanation.definitionFit: His famous letter formally charged officials with injustice, so he was laying blame on them in print.

clue.text: Goodbye sire all of a heap

indicators.note: all of a heap is an idiom for tumbled into disorder, so the word before it is jumbled; its last word doubles as definition

blocks.note: congé is a farewell or dismissal, borrowed from French
these four letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A father collapses in a heap after saying farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word serves twice: the whole phrase signals disorder, and the word heap is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A congeries is a disorderly collection or accumulation of things piled together, which is what a heap means.

blocks.note: UP is the standard abbreviation for this Indian state
on as in go on, move forward

explanation.surface: An exclamation praising progress in a northern Indian state.
explanation.walkthrough: Super is read in its Latin sense, as in superscript or superimpose, not as the slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin preposition super means over or on top of, the same as the English word for resting on something.

blocks.note: Diana was the Roman moon goddess, so to be lunar is to be inside her

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IN DIANA; Diana, goddess of the moon, stands for the moon itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty United States, in the Midwest with Indianapolis as its capital.

blocks.note: first meaning: mocked or ridiculed
second meaning: what you do to a tent, fixing it with ropes

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest a tent being put up; guy also means to make fun of someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy is to ridicule someone, and guy ropes secure a tent, so a pitched tent has been fastened this way.

blocks.note: surface reading: a farm worker returning home at evening
setter's reading: Gray's Elegy says the ploughman homeward makes his weary way, and the poem's verb is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard opens with a weary ploughman trudging home, and every British schoolchild once knew the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's ploughman walks home slowly and heavily, which is exactly how one trudges at the day's end.

blocks.note: first meaning: in music, a note neither sharp nor flat
second meaning: in card games such as pontoon, a winning two-card hand dealt at once

explanation.walkthrough: Note of hand sounds like a promissory note; read the two words separately as a music term and a card term.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the unaltered pitch is so called, and in blackjack an ace with a ten-card scores twenty-one outright.

clue.text: When some of our Colonials courted hydrophobia

definitions.text: When some of our Colonials courted hydrophobia

blocks.clueFragment: When some of our Colonials courted hydrophobia
blocks.note: surface reading: a question about settlers risking rabies
setter's reading: Noël Coward's song says only mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun

explanation.surface: British settlers abroad flirting with rabies.
explanation.walkthrough: Hydrophobia is an old name for rabies, the madness of mad dogs; Coward's song mocks Englishmen in the tropics who walk out at the hottest time.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's mad dogs and Englishmen go out under the hottest sun, which is the twelve o'clock hour.

clue.text: One that has not a crop, 16 Takes District Line port-but a rumen

definitions.text: One that has not a crop

blocks.clueFragment: One that has not a crop
blocks.note: surface reading: a field left unsown for a season
padding: a printing error spliced part of the 16 down clue into this one, and it plays no part
setter's reading: a ruminant animal, which has a rumen for chewing the cud rather than the crop a bird has

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has text from 16 down spliced into it; the real clue reads One that has not a crop but a rumen. Crop is both a harvest and a bird's food pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: A fallow field bears no harvest, and a deer is a ruminant with a rumen, so this animal combines both.

blocks.note: surface reading: an ordinary stick of no value
setter's reading: a slender stick, plain in itself, such as a conjuror's prop or an official's staff

explanation.surface: Dismissing a plain stick as worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender straight stick or staff, whether a magician's prop or a conductor's baton, is exactly a simple rod.

blocks.note: first meaning: a plant or creature that keeps close to the soil
second meaning: a hearer at Shakespeare's Globe theatre who stood in the cheap pit

explanation.walkthrough: Heather is not the moorland plant but one who hears; the Globe is Shakespeare's theatre, where the poorest audience stood on the yard floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a creeping plant or bottom-dwelling fish, and Hamlet uses it for the standing spectators in the theatre pit.

indicators.note: could be offers a possible rearrangement, saying the words before it can become something else

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A typesetter's note that a man's name could be corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue cuts off after cor-, presumably corrected: a broken word is itself something in need of fixing.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors, so a corrected passage has been revised in that way.

clue.text: Takes District Line portmanteau for debt?

definitions.text: Takes District Line portmanteau for debt?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone seizing a travelling bag on the London Underground
setter's reading: a portmanteau word blending District with the trains that run on that line

explanation.surface: A bailiff on the London Underground seizing a passenger's suitcase to settle a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: The District Line is a London Underground route; a portmanteau is both a suitcase and a word made by fusing two others.
explanation.definitionFit: To distrain is to seize someone's goods legally so as to force payment of money owed, chiefly rent.

indicators.note: an outcome is what something turns into, so the words named are rebuilt into a new result

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ruefully asking whether a series of raids achieved nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the letters come from the raids, and the answer is what raids make.
explanation.definitionFit: Inroads are hostile incursions into territory, so successful raids produce them as their result.

blocks.note: surface reading: the moves dancers make to avoid bumping into each other
setter's reading: evasions in general, avoiding a question or an obligation

explanation.walkthrough: On a packed floor dancers shuffle sideways to avoid collisions; the same word means evasions of a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral steps avoid a blow or a collision, and figuratively they are evasions of awkward issues or duties.

blocks.note: surface reading: a historical revolt in the Suffolk town of Bury St Edmunds
setter's reading: an ancient burial, rising up from the ground as a mound

explanation.walkthrough: Bury is an English town name, but here it is the verb: an ancient burial place heaped up as a raised mound.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumulus is a prehistoric earth mound raised over a grave, also called a barrow.

blocks.note: first meaning: a rabble-rouser who stirs up crowds
second meaning: a member of a criminal crew, the old swell pickpocket

explanation.definitionFit: The word is Victorian slang for a well-dressed thief working with confederates, and literally a man who leads crowds.

blocks.note: first meaning: walked heavily and stiffly
second meaning: in cricket, out because the keeper broke the stumps while the batsman was out of his ground

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a wicket-keeper dismisses a batsman this way when he steps out of his crease and misses the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means walked with heavy stomping steps, and in cricket it names one way a batsman is put out.

clue.text: A. in fore you try settled in advance

blocks.note: surface reading: the printed text is garbled and its wordplay cannot be reliably recovered
setter's reading: paid before the goods or service are delivered

explanation.walkthrough: The first half of this clue appears corrupted in the source; fore points to the prefix meaning before.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepay a bill is to discharge it ahead of time, before it falls due.

blocks.note: first meaning: shillings, old British coins
second meaning: Field Marshal Lord Roberts, whose soldiers' nickname for him was this

explanation.walkthrough: FM is not radio but Field Marshal; a bob was a shilling, a coin worth one twentieth of a pound before 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob is slang for a shilling coin, and Bobs was the affectionate name for Field Marshal Frederick Roberts.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone realising something about a lottery
setter's reading: the sweep's stake, a stick with bundled twigs tied around it

explanation.walkthrough: Twigs looks like slang for understands, and sweepstake like a lottery; read it as a stake for sweeping wrapped in twigs.
explanation.definitionFit: A besom is a broom made of a bundle of birch twigs tied around a handle, a traditional sweeping tool.

blocks.note: first meaning: without basis or justification
second meaning: instant coffee leaves no sediment of beans in the cup

explanation.definitionFit: An unjustified claim lacks a basis, and soluble coffee leaves no dregs, the sediment called grounds.

clue.text: American edition, not a new one

blocks.note: US for the United States
ed. is the standard abbreviation for edition

explanation.surface: A bookseller notes that the American printing is a second-hand copy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something second-hand has already had an owner, so it is old rather than fresh from the shop.

indicators.note: confounded means thrown into confusion, so the name beside it is scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Florence baffling her friend Nora.
explanation.walkthrough: Florence reads as a woman's name but is the Italian city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arno is the Tuscan river on whose banks Florence stands, so the city sits on it.

clue.text: Swordsman's strange setback in the wilds of Asia

indicators.note: a setback sends something backwards, so the word strange's synonym is read right to left
the wilds are untamed and disordered, so the place name following is rearranged
in places one piece inside the other, wrapped by the scrambled letters

blocks.note: rum is British slang for odd or peculiar
taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A swordsman suffers an odd misfortune somewhere in the remote Asian wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum meaning odd is everyday British usage; turned round and placed inside a jumbled ASIA it gives SA-MUR-AI.
explanation.definitionFit: A samurai was a member of Japan's warrior class, famed for fighting with the katana blade.

clue.text: State of orphaned Emma, I reckon

indicators.note: an orphan has lost a parent, so the name following loses its mother

blocks.note: taken as written; losing ma, a mother, leaves the first two letters
taken as written
to rate is to reckon or estimate

explanation.surface: Someone guesses at the condition of a girl called Emma who has lost her parents.
explanation.walkthrough: Ma is the familiar word for mother, so orphaned Emma loses MA and leaves EM.
explanation.definitionFit: An emirate is a country or territory ruled by an emir, such as those of the Gulf.

clue.text: Beast that could have pre- rented the Fall?

blocks.clueFragment: Beast that could have pre- rented the Fall?
blocks.note: surface reading: an animal that might have averted mankind's expulsion from Eden
setter's reading: the Fall began with the serpent, and this animal is famous for killing snakes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is misprinted; it means prevented. Had a snake-killer been in the Garden of Eden, the serpent would never have tempted Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: A mongoose is a small carnivorous mammal of Africa and Asia, renowned for killing cobras.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone giving the Babylonian king a dinner invitation
setter's reading: in Daniel the mad king ate grass like an ox, so feeding him means pasturing

explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar was driven out to eat grass like cattle; to take in animals to graze for a fee is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To agist is to take in other people's livestock to feed on one's pasture in return for payment.
